endorsements.quote: Additionally, continuous validation and periodic audits can help identify performance discrepancies across different demographic groups when the AI model is tested in real-world settings.
Ensuring that training datasets are diverse and representative of varied demographic, geographical, and socioeconomic backgrounds is one primary method to reduce potential bias.

Adhering to standardized protocols and undergoing regular training on AI compliance, ethics, and the limitations of AI tools is essential for ensuring that pathologists can integrate these technologies responsibly within their clinical practice.
Institutions must ensure that pathologists and laboratory staff members are regularly updated on evolving AI regulations at the institutional, national, and global levels.

Therefore, it is essential that pathologists remain actively engaged in diagnostic tasks—particularly those that demand critical human insight—and retain control over decision-making thresholds to reinforce accountability and protect the integrity of diagnostic workflows.

This could include implementing AI performance audits that evaluate the accuracy, consistency, and relevance of AI outputs in real-world cases, ensuring that these tools continue to meet clinical standards.

While AI may take on more routine tasks and alleviate workloads in high-volume screenings, it must remain subject to robust human oversight to ensure that critical cases requiring expert review are not bypassed.
For pathology, the lesson from history is clear: ensuring that AI remains a tool for augmentation will require concerted efforts to involve pathologists directly in AI development and oversight.
First, pathologists should engage in governance frameworks within healthcare institutions, advocating for standards that ensure AI is implemented ethically and responsibly.

Key strategies include mandating explainability in AI systems, requiring continual human oversight for critical diagnostic tasks, and instituting iterative validation processes to ensure alignment with clinical and ethical standards.
Hospitals and pathology departments play a key role by establishing oversight policies tailored to their specific workflows and patient populations.

This could include establishing pathologist-led advisory boards to oversee AI applications, forming dedicated research partnerships with AI developers to ensure that patient outcomes and clinical needs are prioritized and creating continuous feedback channels that allow pathologists to adapt AI systems according to evolving clinical and ethical considerations.
Moving forward, expanding these initiatives through online platforms, collaborations with patient advocacy groups, and interactive Q&A sessions can further build public trust.

unlisted_practices: Constrain AI systems so they cannot autonomously adjust thresholds for human review; only pathologists should control such parameters.
Regulators should require periodic reassessment and revalidation of AI tools rather than keeping algorithms locked post-approval.
Harmonize AI standards internationally, for example through the WHO.
Establish protocols for recalibrating AI models based on demographic shifts or healthcare trends.
Incorporate AI competencies into pathology education curricula and continuing professional development.
Use hybrid AI-human training workflows with mentorship so junior pathologists develop independent diagnostic skills.
Implement stringent cybersecurity measures and regulatory compliance to protect patient data in pathology AI systems.
